about.title: Variables on Both Sides: One, None or Infinitely Many Solutions
about.length_note: About 35 minutes, a little over a half-hour class. There are four topics, and each one has a check question. The last topic, writing your own equations, needs a bit more time. You can pause after any beat and pick up again later.

sources.title: 8.3 Solve Equations with Variables and Constants on Both Sides - Prealgebra 2e
5.2 Linear Equations in One Variable with Applications - Contemporary Mathematics

Solve Systems of Linear Equations with Two Variables

say.text: Welcome back. Today you'll learn what to do when x shows up on both sides of an equals sign.

show.text: Variables on Both Sides: One, None or Infinitely Many Solutions

say.text: Go at your own speed. Pause after any step. Every idea gets an example and then a question.

show.text:
1. Collect the x terms
2. Read how the equation ends
3. Why 'none' and 'infinitely many' happen
4. Write your own equations

say.text: First, a reminder from last class. An equation is a balance. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other.

show.text: Balance: do the same to both sides

say.text: Now look at this one: 5x + 3 = 2x + 12. There's an x on the left and an x on the right.
To solve it, we collect the variable terms on one side. We do that by subtracting 2x from both sides.
Now it's a normal equation. Subtract 3 from both sides to get 3x = 9. Then divide by 3.
Always check. Put 3 in the original. The left is 5(3) + 3 = 18. The right is 2(3) + 12 = 18. They match.

show.text:
Left: 5(3) + 3 = 18
Right: 2(3) + 12 = 18
Both are 18, so x = 3 works.

say.text: Your turn. Solve 6x + 1 = 2x + 9.

ask.why: Subtract 2x from both sides to get 4x + 1 = 9. Subtract 1 to get 4x = 8. Divide by 4 to get x = 2. Check: 6(2) + 1 = 13 and 2(2) + 9 = 13. x = 1 comes from adding 2x instead of subtracting it. x = 8 forgets the last step, dividing by 4.

say.text: You can collect the x terms on either side. Try 3x + 10 = 7x − 6. Subtract 3x from both sides.
The x ended up on the right, and that's fine. x = 4 is the same as 4 = x. Check: 3(4) + 10 = 22 and 7(4) − 6 = 22.

show.text: Either side works. Keep every step balanced.

ask.q: In 3x + 10 = 7x − 6, you subtract 3x from both sides. What do you get?
ask.why: On the left, 3x − 3x is 0, so only the 10 is left. On the right, 7x − 3x is 4x, and the −6 stays. 10x comes from adding the x terms instead of subtracting. The last wrong choice only changed the right side. The balance rule says to do it to both sides.

say.text: Now the big idea. Once you collect the x terms, the equation ends in one of three ways.

show.text:
x = a number
a = b (two different numbers)
a = a (the same number twice)

say.text: Way one: x equals a number, like x = 3. Exactly one number works. That is one solution.
Way two is odd. Take 2x + 10 = 2x. Subtract 2x from both sides and the x disappears. You get 10 = 0.
10 does not equal 0. That is a false statement. No value of x can fix it, so there is no solution.
Try one. Solve 4x + 5 = 4x + 9 by subtracting 4x from both sides.

ask.q: Subtract 4x from both sides of 4x + 5 = 4x + 9. What does that tell you?
ask.right: You get 5 = 9, which is false, so there is no solution.
wrong: You get 5 = 9, so there are infinitely many solutions.
ask.why: Both x terms cancel and leave 5 = 9. 5 and 9 are different numbers, so the statement is false for every x. An equation that ends in a false statement has no solution. x = 4 is tempting because of the 4x, but x is gone by then.

say.text: Way three. Take 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10. First distribute the 2 on the left.
Now subtract 2x from both sides. You get 10 = 10. That is always true.
A true statement means any value of x works. Try x = 0, x = 7 or x = −100. They all work. So there are infinitely many solutions.
One warning. If you get 0 = 0, that does not mean x = 0. The x vanished, so every number works. Read the statement that is left.

show.text: x gone? Read what's left: true or false?

ask.q: Solve 6x − 4 = 2(3x − 2). How many solutions does it have?
ask.why: Distribute the 2 on the right to get 6x − 4. Now both sides are 6x − 4. Subtracting 6x from both sides gives −4 = −4, which is true. A true statement means every x works. x = 0 is a trap, because x disappeared.

say.text: Why does 'none' happen? Here's a story. Ava has $10 and saves $3 a week. Ben has $15 and also saves $3 a week.

show.text: Two piggy banks. Ava's starts at $10 and Ben's at $15. Each grows by $3 every week.

say.text: Will they ever have the same amount? Set the two totals equal: 10 + 3w = 15 + 3w. Subtract 3w and you get 10 = 15. False.
They gain the same amount each week, so the $5 gap never changes. No solution means the two sides can never match.

show.text: Same growth, different start → they never meet

ask.q: Why is there no week when Ava and Ben have the same amount?
ask.right: They save the same amount each week, so Ben's $5 head start never shrinks.
wrong: Ben saves more each week, so he is always far ahead.
They would only match in a week that has already passed.
Ava would have to save $0 a week.
ask.why: Each week both totals go up by $3, so the $5 gap stays the same. That is why the weeks cancel and leave the false statement 10 = 15. Ben does not save more per week. The $3 is the same for both.

say.text: This shows up again with lines. Two lines with the same slope but different starting points run side by side. They are parallel and never cross.

show.text: Parallel lines: no point on both

say.text: Now 'infinitely many'. Suppose both friends start with $10 and save $3 a week. Then 10 + 3w = 10 + 3w.

show.text:
Ava: 10 + 3w
Ben: 10 + 3w
Same plan, written twice

say.text: Both sides are the same thing. They match every week, so every value of w is a solution. On a graph, it would be one line drawn on top of itself.

show.text: Same expression on both sides → always true

ask.q: Which equation has infinitely many solutions?
ask.why: 3(x + 4) becomes 3x + 12, which is exactly the right side, so both sides are the same. 3x + 12 = 3x + 4 ends in 12 = 4, which is false, so there is no solution. 3x + 12 = 4x + 12 gives x = 0. 3x + 12 = x + 12 gives 2x = 0, so x = 0 too.

say.text: Here's a quick shortcut. After simplifying, compare the x parts and the plain numbers. Then use it to check your steps.

show.text:
Different x parts → one solution
Same x parts, different numbers → no solution
Same x parts, same numbers → infinitely many

ask.why: The x parts differ (8x and 5x), so x stays and there is one answer. Subtract 5x to get 3x − 3 = 12. Add 3 to get 3x = 15, so x = 5. Check: 8(5) − 3 = 37 and 5(5) + 12 = 37.

say.text: Last topic: writing your own. The standard asks you to give examples with one, none or infinitely many solutions. You can build them.

show.text: Build it so it ends the way you want

say.text: For one solution, make the x parts different. For example, 3x + 4 = x + 10. Subtract x to get 2x + 4 = 10, so 2x = 6 and x = 3.
For no solution, start with a left side like 4x + 3. Write the right side with the same x part, 4x, but a different number: 4x + 8.

show.text:
4x + 3 = 4x + 8
Same x part, different number
3 = 8, so no solution

say.text: For infinitely many, make the two sides equal. You can copy the left side, or write it in disguise: 4x + 3 = 2(2x + 1) + 1. The right side simplifies to 4x + 3.
Try it. Fill in the blank so there is no solution.

ask.q: Which right side makes 5x + 2 = ___ have no solution?
ask.why: No solution needs the same x part (5x) and a different number. 5x + 7 gives 2 = 7, which is false. 5x + 2 gives 2 = 2, which is true, so that is infinitely many. 2x + 7 and 7x + 2 have different x parts, so each gives exactly one solution.

say.text: One more build. This time, aim for infinitely many solutions.

ask.q: Which right side makes 6x + 4 = ___ have infinitely many solutions?
ask.why: 2(3x + 2) becomes 6x + 4, which is the left side exactly, so the statement is always true. 2(3x + 4) becomes 6x + 8 and 3(2x + 2) becomes 6x + 6. Both have the same x part but a different number, so there is no solution. 3(3x + 2) becomes 9x + 6, which has a different x part, so there is one solution.

say.text: Let's gather it up. Collect the x terms, then read the ending.

show.text:
x = number → one solution
False statement (a = b) → no solution
True statement (a = a) → infinitely many solutions

say.text: Well done. Next class is about what a function is. It builds on the idea of one input giving one output.
